claims.claim: When someone you love dies, it is right to grieve openly and deeply, even with the hope of the resurrection.

stances.summary: Christians who die are not lost but sent on ahead. We should miss them, not mourn them. Wearing black for them tells unbelievers that we do not believe what we preach.
stances.quote: our brethren who are freed from this world by the Lord's summons are not to be lamented, since we know that they are not lost, but sent before; that, departing from us, they precede us as travellers, as navigators are accustomed to do; that they should be desired, but not bewailed
stances.original: fratres nostros non esse lugendos accersitione Dominica de saeculo liberatos, cum sciamus non eos amitti sed praemitti, recedentes praecedere, ut proficiscentes, ut navigantes solent, desiderari eos debere, non plangi
stances.context: Written at Carthage during the plague of about 252 to steady a frightened church. Cyprian says God had often revealed and commanded that he preach this publicly. The same sentence goes on: 'that the black garments should not be taken upon us here, when they have already taken upon them white raiment there', and warns that mourning the dead as lost gives pagans a fair charge that our faith is 'simulated, feigned, counterfeit'. Chapter 22: whoever is going to Christ 'ought not to mourn nor lament'. Orthodox bishop, martyred 258. No change of mind recorded. Latin from Latin Wikisource, De mortalitate (Cyprianus Carthaginensis), 20: https://la.wikisource.org/wiki/De_mortalitate_(Cyprianus_Carthaginensis).

stances.summary: The resurrection is certain, so grief for the dead has no ground. Long for them, yes. Lament them, no. Even the longing must be kept patient.
stances.quote: For why should you grieve, if you believe that (your loved one) is not perished? Why should you bear impatiently the temporary withdrawal of him who you believe will return? That which you think to be death is departure. He who goes before us is not to be lamented, though by all means to be longed for.
stances.original: Cur enim doleas, si perisse non credis? Cur inpatienter feras subductum interim quem credis reuersurum? Profectio est quam putas mortem. Non est lugendus qui antecedit, sed plane desiderandus.
stances.context: The chapter is headed 'Of Patience Under Bereavement'. It refuses to excuse grief even where 'some assertion of a right to grief acts the patron to it', and concludes that 'grief for death is needless, and impatience of grief is needless'. It adds: 'That longing also must be tempered with patience', and 'we wound Christ when we accept not with equanimity the summoning out of this world of any by Him'. Written about 200 to 206, before his Montanist period (his later heterodox years). In chapter 1 he admits he is 'all unfit' to practise the patience he recommends. Latin from tertullian.org's Latin text, 9.3 (the page prints the paragraph marker [3] before 'Cur enim'): https://www.tertullian.org/latin/de_patientia.htm.

stances.summary: Tears for the dead are not a sin. Natural grief is different from the sadness of unbelief. Jesus wept, and so do I. But a believer's tears should end, and grief should be moderated or kept private.
stances.quote: But we have not incurred any grievous sin by our tears. Not all weeping proceeds from unbelief or weakness. Natural grief is one thing, distrustful sadness is another, and there is a very great difference between longing for what you have lost and lamenting that you have lost it.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, NPNF 2nd series vol. 10, 1896
stances.original: At non gravem lacrymis contraximus culpam: non omnis infidelitatis aut infirmitatis est fletus. Alius est naturae dolor, alia est tristitia diffidentiae: et plurimum refert desiderare, quod habueris; et lugere, quod amiseris.
stances.work: On the Death of Satyrus (De excessu fratris sui Satyri)
stances.context: Book 1 is the funeral oration for his brother Satyrus at Milan (378). He weeps openly and defends it: 'I confess, then, that I too wept, but the Lord also wept.' Yet near the end of Book 1 he checks himself: 'So, then, my tears shall cease' and 'Let them, therefore, weep who cannot have the hope of the resurrection', then admits his tears cannot wholly cease. Book 2 ('On belief in the resurrection'), preached at the grave a week later, argues the other side: 'we deem that death is not to be mourned over' and 'Put aside your grief, if you can; if you cannot, keep it to yourself.' A deliberate middle: tears are innocent, lasting or public lament is not. Latin from Latin Wikisource, De excessu fratris sui Satyri 1.10: https://la.wikisource.org/wiki/De_excessu_fratris_sui_Satyri.

stances.summary: Grief for those we love is natural and not blameworthy, and Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb. But a believer's grief should be short, and should not look like the grief of those without hope.
stances.quote: There is nothing in the sorrow of mortals over their dearly beloved dead which merits displeasure; but the sorrow of believers ought not to be prolonged.
stances.original: Non quidem succensendum est de caris mortuis dolori mortalium; sed diuturnus dolor non debet esse fidelium.
stances.context: Written (date unknown) to Sapida, a consecrated virgin whose brother Timothy, a deacon of the church of Carthage, had died. He goes on: the Lord's weeping for Lazarus 'by His example permitted, though He did not by any precept enjoin, the shedding of tears over the graves even of those regarding whom we believe that they shall rise again'. Elsewhere: in Confessions 4 he calls his own youthful, inconsolable grief for a friend a kind of madness ('O madness, which know not how to love men as men should be loved!'). At his mother Monica's funeral (387) he held back tears in public, because 'we did not consider it fitting to celebrate that funeral with tearful plaints and groanings', then wept alone and asks readers not to laugh at him for it (Confessions 9.12). City of God 14.9 rejects freedom from emotion in this life: 'we are rather worse men than better if we have none of these emotions at all'. So: tears yes, but brief, and not wailing. Latin from augustinus.it, Epistola 263.3 (https://www.augustinus.it/latino/lettere/lettera_272_testo.htm; the site refuses plain scripted requests without browser headers).

stances.summary: Scripture tells us not to grieve for those who have fallen asleep, because that grief belongs to people without hope. Tears belong to prayer, not to the loss of a loved one.
stances.quote: She quoted the Apostle's words about the duty of not being grieved for them that sleep; because only men without hope have such feelings.
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 5, 1893
stances.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection, by her brother Gregory of Nyssa
stances.context: Gregory reports her words from his visit some nine months after their brother Basil's death (379), when she lay dying; this is his report of her teaching, not a verbatim speech. She first let him grieve 'for a little while, like a skilful driver', then 'tried to check me by speaking, and to correct with the curb of her reasonings the disorder of my soul'. The same stance runs through his Life of Macrina (W.K. Lowther Clarke's translation, SPCK 1916, public domain in the US: https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/gregory_macrina_1_life.htm). When her brother Naucratius was killed she, 'conquering nature', kept their mother from crying out, tearing her dress or singing funeral chants. At her own death her nuns had held back 'their impulse to mourn for fear of her'. Gregory recalls her rule that the one proper time for tears is prayer: 'recommending us to weep at the time of prayer'.

stances.summary: A heart on fire with loss needs the release of tears, and he mourned openly. But he also checked his own weeping as more than was right, and accepted his sister's correction.
stances.quote: In no other way can the burning heart cool down, swelling as it is with its affliction, unless it relieves itself by sobs and tears.
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 5, 1893
stances.location: the lament, just after 'Call for the mourning women'
stances.context: Preached at Constantinople in 381 for Meletius of Antioch, who died during the Council. After a long public lament he checks himself in the same paragraph: 'But let me have all tears wiped away, for I feel that I am indulging more than is right in this womanish sorrow for our loss.' In On the Soul and the Resurrection (about 380) he casts himself as the mourner whose 'passionate grief' Macrina corrects. In the Life of Macrina he 'gave myself up to lamentation' at her death, then called on the nuns to turn 'the lamentations into psalmody'. He practises open grief and defends its release, while accepting that it must be reined in.

stances.summary: Christians who have put on Christ ought not to grieve for the dead who are with Him. Grief without limits is unbelief, and it gives the enemies of the faith something to mock.
stances.quote: Yours are detestable tears, sacrilegious tears, unbelieving tears; for they know no limits, and bring you to the verge of death.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 6, 1893
stances.original: Detestandae sunt istae lacrymae, plenae sacrilegio, incredulitate plenissimae, quae non habent modum, quae usque ad viciniam mortis accedunt.
stances.work: Letter 39, to Paula, on the death of Blaesilla
stances.context: Written at Rome in 384 (the New Advent header prints 389) to Paula, whose daughter Blaesilla had died; Paula fainted at the funeral and was starving herself. Jerome wept too ('this entire letter is written in tears') and grants 'I pardon you the tears of a mother, but I ask you to restrain your grief.' His principle, section 4: 'we ought not to grieve for the dead.' Twelve years later (Letter 60, 396, to Heliodorus) he is the same but gentler: 'Shall I join my tears to yours? The apostle forbids me', yet 'tears flow down my cheeks'; he admits Lazarus's sisters and Jesus wept, but asks 'Set a limit, I pray you, to your sorrow' and tells a bishop 'If a king may not weep, neither may a bishop'. Letter 108 (404), on Paula's own death: 'if we persist in weeping for one who reigns with Christ, we shall seem to envy her her glory.' Latin from the Patrologia text reproduced on remacle.org: https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/eglise/jerome/paula2.htm.

stances.summary: Lamenting the dead is what people without hope do. If you believe in the resurrection, why wail? Weep gently if you must, but honour the dead with psalms, hymns and almsgiving, not with mourning.
stances.quote: For a soul that knows nothing of the Resurrection, but thinks that this death is death, naturally afflicts itself, and bewails and mourns intolerably as for lost ones. But you, who expectest a resurrection, on what account do you lament? To lament then is the part of those who have no hope.
stances.translation: John A. Broadus, NPNF 1st series vol. 13, 1889
stances.context: He preached this again and again. Homily 62 on John makes a concession: 'No, neither do I forbid weeping, but I forbid the beating yourselves, the weeping immoderately', and 'weep, but gently, but with decency, but with the fear of God'. But he adds that he says this 'not as giving a rule of action, but as condescending (to human infirmity)'. In Homily 4 on Hebrews he threatens anyone who hires professional mourning women: 'that person we will exclude from the Church for a long time, as we do the idolater'. In To a Young Widow he waited until he had 'permitted you to take your fill of mourning' before consoling her. Much of his fire is aimed at public wailing, which he says makes pagans laugh at the resurrection.

stances.summary: Only a heart of stone would feel a death lightly, and I wept too. But God commands believers not to grieve like those without hope, so keep your grief without letting it overwhelm you.
stances.quote: Be an example of fortitude to other women, and so regulate your grief that you may neither eject it from your heart, nor be overwhelmed by your distress.
stances.work: Letter 269, to the wife of Arinthaeus the general (consolatory)
stances.context: His letters of consolation hold both sides. Letter 5, to Nectarius on the death of his son: 'I need not tell you how I sighed and wept. Who could be so stony-hearted, so truly inhuman, as to be insensible to what has occurred, or be affected by merely moderate grief?' Yet in the same letter: 'it is God's command that we who trust in Christ should not grieve over them who are fallen asleep'. Letter 6, to the boy's mother, holds up the Maccabean mother who saw her sons die 'without a sigh, without even shedding one unworthy tear'. Letter 28, to a bereaved church: 'If lament you must, (which I do not allow, lest you be in this respect like them which have no hope,)'. Letter 29: 'Now I have mourned, as none could help mourning'. Basil died in 379. Letters 300 to 302, also consolatory, are only summarised in NPNF and were not used.

stances.summary: Scripture itself tells us to let tears fall over the dead, so feeling nothing is wrong. But lamenting more than is good is wrong too. The Christian walks between coldness and excess.
stances.quote: For I am neither going to lament for him who is gone more than is good— as I should not approve of such conduct even in others — nor am I going to praise him beyond due measure.
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894
stances.work: Oration 7, funeral oration on his brother Caesarius
stances.context: Preached about 369 at the burial of his younger brother, a court physician. He then cites Sirach 38:16, 'Let tears fall down over the dead, and begin to lament', as 'removing us equally from insensibility and immoderation'. He admits that at one memory 'my feelings have overcome my philosophic restraint' (section 6), and turns the grief at the end: 'Let us not then mourn Cæsarius but ourselves' (section 20). His orations for his sister Gorgonia (8) and his father (18) follow the same pattern of praise, tears and consolation.

stances.summary: Faced with a child's death, love pulls two ways. Faith says rejoice, family love says weep, and both are right. But weeping too much for a soul that is happy with God becomes a fault.
stances.quote: Alas, what shall I do? I struggle, hanging between two kinds of love. Should I rejoice or grieve? The boy deserves both. Love urges tears on me, and love urges joy; but faith bids me rejoice, and family love bids me weep.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (MQDQ text; critical edition W. Hartel, CSEL 30, 1894)
stances.original: Heu! quid agam? dubia pendens pietate laboro, Gratuler an doleam? dignus utroque puer; Cuius amor lacrimas et amor mihi gaudia suadet, Sed gaudere fides, flere iubet pietas.
stances.work: Poem 31, consolation to Pneumatius and Fidelis on the death of their son Celsus
stances.context: A long consolation (over 600 lines; date uncertain) written to parents whose son Celsus died in his eighth year. The MQDQ page prints the verse number 10 between the third and fourth lines quoted. A little later (lines 43-46, own rendering) he warns them: 'Loving parents, spare yourselves, I beg, from sinning through many tears, so that your devotion does not turn into guilt. For it is an impious devotion to mourn a blessed soul, and a harmful love to weep for one who rejoices in God.' Latin: 'Parcite quaeso, pii, multis peccare, parentes, Fletibus, in culpam ne pietas ueniat. Impia nam pietas animam lugere beatam Gaudentemque deo flere nocens amor est.' The only published English (P.G. Walsh, Ancient Christian Writers 40, 1975) is in copyright and was not used. Letter 13, his consolation to Pammachius on the death of his wife, reportedly takes the same line, but only a modern translation was found, so it is not quoted here.

stances.summary: To feel nothing at a death is pride, not strength. Mourning is a debt of love owed to the dead. But grief must stop short of the excess that turns against God.
stances.quote: He was not altogether unmoved, lest by his very insensibility he should shew a contempt of God; nor was he completely in commotion, lest by excess of grief he should commit sin. But because there are two commandments of love, i.e. the love of God, and of our neighbour; that he might discharge the love of our neighbour, he paid the debt of mourning to his sons
stances.translation: anonymous Oxford translation, Library of the Fathers, 1844
stances.work: Morals on the Book of Job (Moralia in Job)
stances.context: Begun as talks to monks at Constantinople and finished as pope, roughly 579 to 595. Commenting on 'Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head', he rejects both those who 'account it a high degree of philosophical fortitude' to feel nothing and those whose grief runs to 'excesses of the tongue'. Job's torn robe and shaved head are praised as the outward, visible sign of real pain. So he defends open mourning within limits. He does not mention the resurrection hope in this passage.

stances.summary: I know a saint in glory should not be mourned, and reason says I should rejoice. But I cannot stop myself grieving, so come and mourn him with me.
stances.quote: And yet I am well aware that such a man ought not to be mourned over, to whom, after his victory and triumph over the world, there has now at last been given the crown of righteousness. Nevertheless, I cannot so command myself as to keep from grieving.
stances.work: Letters, Letter 2, to the deacon Aurelius
stances.context: Not in the results pool: Martin of Tours's friend and biographer, writing about 397 on hearing of Martin's death. He wept 'most abundantly' and begs his friend to come 'that we may mourn in common him whom in common we love'. In Letter 3 (to Bassula), describing Martin's funeral, he pardons those who wept and congratulates those who rejoiced, and says of the virgins there: 'No doubt faith would prevent the shedding of tears, yet affection forced out groans.' Martin himself, in the same letter, 'is said to have burst into tears' when his monks lamented his coming death, but no view of his on mourning is recorded.

stances.summary: When her husband and two sons died together, she shed no tear. She thanked Christ that she was now free to serve Him more readily.
stances.quote: Yet not a tear fell from her eyes. Motionless she stood there; then casting herself at the feet of Christ, she smiled, as though she held Him with her hands. Henceforth, Lord, she said, I will serve You more readily, for You have freed me from a great burden.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 6, 1893
stances.original: Lacrymae gutta non fluxit; stetit immobilis, et ad pedes advoluta Christi, quasi ipsum teneret, arrisit. Expeditius, inquit, tibi servitura sum, Domine, quia tanto me onere liberasti.
stances.context: Not in the results pool. Recorded by Jerome in 384, while she was alive, as a 'modern instance' to shame Paula's grief; he swears 'Christ is my witness that my words are true'. Per Jerome, her husband's body was not yet buried when two of her sons died. Melania the Elder (died about 410), a Roman noblewoman, then sailed east, visited the monks of the Egyptian desert and founded a monastery on the Mount of Olives with Rufinus. Jerome later broke with her circle in the Origenist quarrel, but this passage is his praise. Latin from the Patrologia text on remacle.org: https://remacle.org/bloodwolf/eglise/jerome/paula2.htm.

stances.summary: A monk's true Father cannot die. He holds up as a model the monk who called the news of his father's death blasphemy.
stances.quote: The death of his father was announced to one of the monks: 'Cease your blasphemy,' said he to the person that told him; 'my father is immortal.'
stances.translation: A.C. Zenos, NPNF 2nd series vol. 2, 1890 (Socrates quoting Evagrius)
stances.original: Ἐμηνύθη τινὶ τῶν μοναχῶν θάνατος τοῦ πατρός· ὁ δὲ πρὸς τὸν ἀπαγγείλαντα͵ παῦσαι͵ φησί͵ βλασφημῶν· ὁ γὰρ ἐμὸς πατὴρ ἀθάνατός ἐστιν.
stances.work: Praktikos (The Monk), quoted in Socrates Scholasticus, Church History
stances.context: Socrates inserts a run of sayings and closes: 'These few extracts from Evagrius we thought it would be appropriate to insert here.' Evagrius introduces them as examples to follow: 'It becomes us to enquire into the habits of the pious monks who have preceded us, in order that we may correct ourselves by their example'. The monk is unnamed. The stance is Evagrius's because he offers the answer as a model. Greek (Praktikos 95) from Luke Dysinger's Praktikos page: https://www.ldysinger.com/Evagrius/01_Prak/01_Praktikos.htm (its facing English is modern and was not used). Heterodox status: Evagrius's Origenist teaching was condemned in 553; his ascetic works stayed widely read.

stances.summary: Weeping at the tomb helps no one. Pour those tears into prayer in church instead, because that profits both the dead and the living.
stances.quote: Instead of the tears that profit not, which are at the tomb: pour them forth in your prayer, in the midst of the Church.
stances.translation: J.T. Sarsfield Stopford, NPNF 2nd series vol. 13, 1890
stances.context: In Hymns 61 to 62 most of the words are spoken by Death, a dramatic device. Ephrem introduces him: 'In wisdom let us hearken to Death, O my beloved: how he accuses us for our weeping, and for our mourning.' So the rebuke is Ephrem's teaching in Death's mouth. The next stanza: 'weep not with a weeping that afflicts, both dead and living!' Hymn 66.14: 'If there be a resurrection: weep not, neither labour as though strangers.' Ephrem (died 373) is honoured East and West; these hymns are translated from the Syriac.

stances.summary: The mature Christian loves his dearest with a love that rejoices when they go home to God. Peter did not mourn his wife as she was led to death. He cheered her on.
stances.quote: They say, accordingly, that the blessed Peter, on seeing his wife led to death, rejoiced on account of her call and conveyance home, and called very encouragingly and comfortingly, addressing her by name, Remember the Lord. Such was the marriage of the blessed and their perfect disposition towards those dearest to them.
stances.context: Written in Alexandria about 200 to 210, as a portrait of the mature Christian, whom Clement calls the true 'Gnostic'. The story is a martyrdom, told as tradition ('They say'); Eusebius repeats it (Church History 3.30). It fits his wider ideal: the perfect Christian 'does not fall into pain, being persuaded that all things happen well' (Stromata 6.9). Clement never discusses ordinary mourning directly, so this is his ideal of the perfect, not a rule for every bereaved believer.

stances.summary: Only three sorrows are good: sorrow for sin, longing for holiness, and longing for heaven. Every other sorrow belongs to this world and should be driven out of the heart.
stances.quote: Wherefore except that sorrow which is endured either for the sake of saving penitence, or for the sake of aiming at perfection, or for the desire of the future, all sorrow and dejection must equally be resisted, as belonging to this world, and being that which works death, and must be entirely expelled from our hearts like the spirit of fornication and covetousness and anger.
stances.translation: Edgar C.S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Book 9 is on dejection (tristitia), one of the eight principal faults, written about 420 for monks in Gaul. He does not name bereavement. But chapter 13 lists sorrow that comes 'from some loss' among the kinds to be overcome by hope of the future. So this is a general rule that covers grief for the dead, not a passage about it. (His teaching on grace was later disputed; that has no bearing here.)

splits_fathers: No early Christian found here defends grief that is both deep and unlimited, so nobody lands cleanly on 'agree'. The real split is between two camps. The first says believers should not mourn their dead at all, or should turn their tears into prayer: Tertullian, Cyprian, Chrysostom in his sermons, Jerome writing to Paula, Macrina, Melania the Elder, the monk Evagrius holds up, Ephrem (through the voice of Death), Clement's ideal Christian, and Cassian's rule on sorrow. The second defends natural, visible tears within limits: Ambrose, Augustine, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa, Paulinus of Nola, Gregory the Great and Sulpicius Severus. Closest to 'agree' are Gregory of Nyssa's lament for Meletius ('In no other way can the burning heart cool down... unless it relieves itself by sobs and tears'), Ambrose's first funeral oration ('I confess, then, that I too wept, but the Lord also wept'), Basil's Letter 5 (who could be 'so stony-hearted' as to feel 'merely moderate grief'?), and Gregory the Great calling mourning 'the debt' love owes the dead. Both camps quote 1 Thessalonians 4:13. The strict read it as forbidding grief; the moderate read it as forbidding only hopeless grief, and point to Jesus weeping at Lazarus's tomb and to Sirach 38:16. Several who forbid grief wept openly themselves (Jerome, Ambrose, Basil, Gregory of Nyssa), while Augustine held back his tears at his mother's funeral and wept alone. So there are strong, citable voices for 'disagree' and for a middle view, and none for grief without limit.
splits_people_today: Today the claim is strongly one-sided toward 'agree'. Most people, Christian or not, see open grief as healthy and holding back tears as unhealthy repression; sayings like 'grief is the price of love' are common, and most churches teach 'grieve, but with hope', usually citing Jesus weeping (John 11:35). A minority lean the other way: some Christians feel that heavy grief at a believer's funeral shows weak faith ('they're in a better place', 'a celebration of life, not a funeral'), and some cultures and families prize composure and a 'stiff upper lip'. As worded, most players will agree, so the statement will separate people only weakly, while it separates the Fathers well (strict against moderate). A version that turns on the Fathers' real dividing lines would discriminate better: whether a believer's grief should be brief, whether it should be private rather than public, or whether loud mourning denies the resurrection. On those, people today split more evenly.

misattributions.line: Death is nothing at all. I have only slipped away into the next room.
misattributions.attributed_to: St Augustine (in French versions also Charles Péguy)
misattributions.truth: From Henry Scott Holland's sermon 'Death the King of Terrors', preached at St Paul's Cathedral in May 1910, after the death of Edward VII. Not in Augustine. In the sermon it is presented as one of two contrasting ways of seeing death, not simply as Holland's own view.

misattributions.line: Ne pleure pas si tu m'aimes / Si tu savais le don de Dieu et ce qu'est le Ciel (Do not weep if you love me; if you knew the gift of God and what heaven is)
misattributions.truth: A French funeral text printed everywhere under Augustine's name, always without a reference. No passage in Augustine's works has been identified for it. Treat as unattributed.

misattributions.line: He whom we love and lose is no longer where he was before. He is now wherever we are.
misattributions.truth: Circulates on memorial and parish sites with no reference to any work of Chrysostom, and none was found. Unverified; do not use.

misattributions.line: Do not grieve that you have lost him, but give thanks that you had him.
misattributions.attributed_to: St Jerome (often quoted loosely and without reference)
misattributions.truth: Genuine in substance. Jerome, Letter 60.7 (to Heliodorus, 396), NPNF: 'Do not grieve that you have lost such a paragon: rejoice rather that he has once been yours.' Latin: 'nec doleas, quod talem amiseris, sed gaudeas, quod talem habueris'. Ambrose says the same of his brother (On the Death of Satyrus 1.3): 'I must rather rejoice that I had such a brother than grieve that I had lost a brother'. Note that Jerome sets it inside a plea to 'Set a limit, I pray you, to your sorrow'.

notes:
1. All quotations were copied from the raw pages with curl and checked by script against those pages, whitespace normalised. The only 'original' that does not match character for character is Paulinus: the MQDQ page prints the verse number 10 between the third and fourth lines quoted. Latin originals come from different pages than the English (the url field holds the English page); each context names the Latin source. Evagrius's Greek is from Luke Dysinger's Praktikos page (https://www.ldysinger.com/Evagrius/01_Prak/01_Praktikos.htm, ch. 95); the English facing it there is modern and was not used. Greek for Basil, both Gregorys, Chrysostom and Clement was not found online in a checkable form, so 'original' is null for them. On New Advent some phrases inside quotations sit in <q> tags (for example Macrina's 'grieved for them that sleep'); browsers may draw quotation marks around them that are not part of the text, so compare against the text with tags removed.
2. Tally: 10 disagree, 8 mixed, 0 agree. The mixed voices are not fence-sitters. Each states a deliberate middle: tears are innocent and even owed, but they must be brief, measured, or private. For scoring, the mixed ones that lean most toward open grief are Gregory of Nyssa (Meletius), Ambrose (Book 1), Gregory the Great and Basil (Letter 5); the most restrictive of the mixed are Augustine (short grief, not public) and Paulinus (too many tears become a fault).
3. The practical programme behind the 'disagree' camp is to redirect tears, not to feel nothing. Macrina: weep at prayer. Ephrem: pour the tears out in prayer in church. Chrysostom: honour the dead with 'hymns and psalmodies and an excellent life' and with alms. At Monica's funeral 'Evodius took up the Psalter'. At Paula's (Jerome, Letter 108): 'No weeping or lamentation followed her death, such as are the custom of the world; but all present united in chanting the psalms'. Abba Poemen, told Arsenius had died, blessed him for having wept over himself in this life (Budge, Paradise of the Holy Fathers, 1907, vol. 2, Sayings no. 152): the desert redirects weeping from the dead to one's own sins.
4. Much of the fire is aimed at public, ritual wailing (hired mourning women, beating the breast, tearing hair and clothes), which pagans also practised. Chrysostom threatened to exclude those who hired mourners. Cyprian and Jerome add a witness argument: grief that looks hopeless lets pagans mock the resurrection. Jerome (Letter 60.14) and Ambrose (Book 2, 'keep it to yourself') add a public and private distinction. A quiz statement about public mourning would track this better than one about feeling grief.
5. Several writers call loud mourning 'womanish' (Gregory of Nyssa on Meletius; Ambrose's Lycian law in Book 2.7; Chrysostom's sermons address women). Do not reproduce that framing in quiz copy.
6. Checked and not counted: Benedict (Gregory's Dialogues 2.34, 1911 edition: seeing his sister Scholastica's soul rise as a dove, he 'rejoicing much to see her great glory, with hymns and lauds gave thanks' — a deed recorded about fifty years later, not a stated view). Lactantius (Divine Institutes 6.15) says the Stoics' removal of grief 'cannot possibly be done' and names the slaughter of friends, but speaks of emotion in general, not of Christian mourning. Pelagius's comment on 1 Thess 4:13 (Souter's edition) is one obscure line and cannot be classified. Paula's own grief is described by Jerome (deep, near fatal), but her own words on it are not recorded. Martin of Tours wept when his monks lamented his coming death (Sulpicius, Letter 3) but left no view on mourning.
7. Nothing relevant found for: Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Origen, Perpetua, Hippolytus, Novatian, Athanasius, Antony, Hilary, Syncletica (her sayings on sorrow concern sadness in general), Moses the Black, Arsenius, Boethius (his Consolation is about misfortune, not bereavement), John Climacus (Ladder Step 7 is on mourning for sin), Isaac the Syrian, Benedict's Rule.
